365.title: The chosen family
365.hook: Allah chose Adam, Nuh, the family of Ibrahim and the family of Imran (3:33)
365.howItsDone: Muslims honor the prophets named in 3:33 and their families, and the story of the family of Imran, Maryam's family, is told at length in the surah that bears its name.

segments.voice: Yesterday: our Lord, don't let our hearts swerve after You guided us. Your line was keep my heart straight. Did you catch a lean and come back? Day three hundred sixty-five.

Some families keep a list somewhere. A page in the front of an old book, a chart someone's aunt made, a grandparent who can recite the names back five generations and gets annoyed when you lose track. Al 'Imran is named after a family, and here, in verse thirty-three, the surah gives its own short list. Four names. It isn't a family tree in the usual sense. It's a list of who was chosen, and it's the doorway to the stories this surah is about to tell.
screen: `A PAGE IN THE FRONT OF AN OLD BOOK.` → `FOUR NAMES.` → `THE DOORWAY TO THE STORIES.`

segments.voice: Pickthall translates 3:33: "Lo! Allah preferred Adam and Noah and the Family of Abraham and the Family of 'Imran above (all His) creatures." Adam, where the human story begins, as the Qur'an tells it. Nuh, Noah, who carried the survivors through the flood. The family of Ibrahim, which runs through Isma'il and Ishaq to a long line of prophets, and, Muslims believe, to Muhammad ﷺ. And the family of Imran. Who is Imran? The Qur'an calls Maryam, the mother of Isa, the daughter of Imran, and many commentators take this to be her father. Others connected the name to Amram, the father of Musa and Harun. The verse itself doesn't say, and both views appear in the classical books. The Arabic verb is istafa, from a root meaning purity, the clear, best part of something. The Prophet's well-known title al-Mustafa, the chosen one, comes from the same root. Then 3:34 adds, in Pickthall's words, "They were descendants one of another." One line, linked from Adam onward. But chosen doesn't mean easy, and the surah shows it right away. The next verses begin with Imran's wife, pregnant, promising her unborn child to God, and then surprised when the child is a girl. That girl is Maryam. Over the next days we'll meet Zakariyya, who looked after her, and the angels who spoke to her. Being chosen, in these stories, isn't a badge. It's a weight passed hand to hand, and each person in the line had to carry it in their own hard moment.
screen: `FOUR NAMES IN ONE VERSE` · `WHO IS IMRAN?` · `ISTAFA: TO CHOOSE THE PUREST` · `A WEIGHT PASSED HAND TO HAND` · then, large: `DESCENDANTS ONE OF ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: When the bell starts, think back along your own line. A parent, a grandparent, someone further back whose name you only half know. And if your family is complicated, think of whoever raised you, taught you, or held you up: a line doesn't have to be only blood. Pick one person and name one thing they passed to you, a habit, a phrase, a way of standing. If you pray, you can thank God for them, in whatever words are yours. The bell holds the time.
The chosen family. Adam, Nuh, the family of Ibrahim and the family of Imran, chosen, and descendants one of another. Today's word.
Your line: a chosen line. Today, tell someone younger one thing you received from someone older, so the line keeps going. Day three hundred sixty-five.

366.title: Zakariyya's silence
366.hook: his sign is three days without speaking except by gesture, and remembering Allah (3:41)
366.tomorrow: Maryam above the women of the worlds
366.howItsDone: Muslims honor Zakariyya and Yahya as prophets; his story (3:37–41 and Surah Maryam) is often recited by those hoping for a child, and his sign of silence filled with remembrance is a model for quiet dhikr in the morning and evening.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the chosen family: Adam, Nuh, the family of Ibrahim and the family of Imran. Your line was a chosen line. Did you pass something on to someone younger? Day three hundred sixty-six.

An old man walks into a small prayer room to check on the girl he's raising. She's Maryam, and he's her guardian, Zakariyya. He finds food beside her, and it's food he didn't bring. Where did this come from, he asks. From God, she says; God provides for whom He wills, beyond counting. And the old man, who has no children and a wife who never could, stands right there and starts to pray for a child of his own.
screen: `A SMALL PRAYER ROOM.` → `FOOD HE DIDN'T BRING.` → `AN OLD MAN STARTS TO PRAY.`

segments.voice: That's 3:37 and 38. The prayer room is called the mihrab, the same word used today for the niche in a mosque's wall that shows the direction of prayer. What Zakariyya saw in Maryam's room made him brave enough to ask. Then, 3:39: while he's still standing in prayer, the angels call to him with good news of a son, Yahya, who will confirm a word from God, and be noble, chaste, and a prophet. And Zakariyya, who has just asked for exactly this, asks how. I'm old. My wife is barren. The answer, in Pickthall's words: "So (it will be). Allah doeth what He will." So he asks for a sign. And the sign is strange. In 3:41 he's told he won't speak to people for three days, except by ramz, by gesture. And then: remember your Lord much, and glorify Him in the evening and the morning. In Surah Maryam, chapter nineteen, the same sign is given as three nights, and there he comes out and signals to his people to glorify God morning and evening. Commentators differ on why it came this way. Some read the silence as a mercy, a sign he could feel in his own body. Others note that his tongue was stopped from talk with people, but never from remembering God. Christians tell a story of the same man, Zechariah, in the Gospel of Luke. Here, in the Qur'an's telling, the point lands on what filled the silence. Three days with no small talk, no explaining, no complaining. Only gestures, and dhikr, remembrance, morning and evening.

segments.voice: Try a short version of Zakariyya's sign. Later today, if you can, take a quiet hour: no talking, no messages, gestures only if someone needs you. For now, when the bell starts, close your mouth gently and let the silence settle. Notice how much talk runs inside you even when you aren't speaking. Each time a sentence starts to form, let it go, and come back to one simple remembrance. If you pray, that can be subhanallah, glory be to God. If you don't, simply the breath. The bell holds the time.
Zakariyya's silence. Three days without speech, only gesture, filled with remembrance, morning and evening. Today's word.
Your line: silent and remembering. Today, when you'd normally fill a pause with talk, leave it empty for a moment, and let one quiet remembrance take its place. Day three hundred sixty-six.

367.title: Maryam above the women of the worlds
367.word: Maryam above the women of the worlds
367.hook: the angels say Allah has chosen and purified her (3:42–43)
367.howItsDone: Muslims hold Maryam in deep honor as the mother of the prophet Isa and, following the hadith, among the best of women; Surah Maryam (19) and her verses in Al 'Imran are recited and taught, and girls are often named after her.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zakariyya's silence: three days of gesture, filled with remembrance. Your line was silent and remembering. Did you leave a pause empty? Day three hundred sixty-seven.

Readers of the Qur'an point out something about Maryam: a queen appears in it, and prophets' wives and mothers, but tradition counts her as the one woman the book calls by her own name. Maryam, the mother of Isa. A whole surah, the nineteenth, carries her name. And here in Al 'Imran, the girl Zakariyya was raising has grown up, and the angels come to speak to her directly, with words that set her above the women of the worlds.
screen: `CALLED BY HER OWN NAME.` → `A SURAH CARRIES HER NAME.` → `THE ANGELS SPEAK TO HER.`

segments.voice: In 3:42 the angels say: O Maryam, God has chosen you and purified you, and chosen you above the women of the worlds. Listen to the shape of it. The word for chosen, istafa, the one we met two days ago with the family of Imran, comes twice. Commentators explain the two choosings differently: some say the first is being chosen for devotion and accepted in the sanctuary, and the second is being chosen above all women, for the birth of Isa. Between them, purified: kept clean of what would stain her. Then 3:43 gives her instructions, the same ones given to any worshiper: be devoutly obedient to your Lord, prostrate, and bow with those who bow. A young woman, alone in a sanctuary, addressed by angels, and told to pray. Verse 44 adds a scene from her childhood: the men of the temple cast their pens, like drawing lots, to decide who would take care of her, and they argued over the honor. Zakariyya won. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is reported, in Sahih al-Bukhari, to have said that the best of the women of her time was Maryam, and the best of the women of his own time was Khadijah, his wife. Another hadith, in Tirmidhi, names four women who are enough, among all the women of the world, to look to: Maryam, Asiya the wife of Pharaoh, Khadijah, and Fatimah his daughter. Christians honor Maryam too, as Mary, and the two traditions tell her story in their own ways. In the Qur'an's telling, her greatness isn't fame. It's two choosings, one purifying, and a life of bowing in prayer.
screen: `CHOSEN, PURIFIED, CHOSEN ABOVE` · `BOW WITH THOSE WHO BOW` · `THE PENS CAST FOR HER` · `MARYAM, ASIYA, KHADIJAH, FATIMAH` · then, large: `ABOVE THE WOMEN OF THE WORLDS.`

segments.voice: When the bell starts, bring to mind a woman of faith you've known or read about. A grandmother who prayed before dawn, a teacher, a neighbor, someone from history. Picture her at prayer, or doing the one thing she did faithfully, year after year. Let yourself feel some honor for her. If you pray, you can ask God's mercy on her. Then think of one way, today, to honor her: tell her story, call her, or do the thing she did. The bell holds the time.

368.title: A common word
368.hook: come to a word common between us: to worship none but Allah (3:64)
368.howItsDone: Muslims cite 3:64 in interfaith conversation; in 2007 Muslim scholars and leaders addressed an open letter titled 'A Common Word Between Us and You' to Christian leaders, built on love of God and love of neighbor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maryam, chosen above the women of the worlds. Your line was chosen and purified. Did you honor a woman of faith out loud? Day three hundred sixty-eight.

In October 2007, a letter went out from Muslim scholars and leaders, more than a hundred and thirty of them, Sunni and Shia, from many countries. It was addressed to the Pope, to Orthodox patriarchs, to the Archbishop of Canterbury, and to the leaders of Christian churches everywhere. Its title was a phrase lifted straight out of a verse in Al 'Imran. The phrase was: a common word between us and you.
screen: `OCTOBER 2007.` → `A LETTER TO CHURCH LEADERS.` → `A PHRASE FROM AL 'IMRAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, 3:64, in Pickthall's words: "Say: O People of the Scripture! Come to an agreement between us and you: that we shall worship none but Allah." Pickthall says agreement. The Arabic is kalimatin sawa', a word that is level, equal, the same for both sides. People of the Scripture, ahl al-kitab, is the Qur'an's name for Jews and Christians, those given scripture before, in the Qur'an's terms. The verse goes on: that we ascribe no partner to God, and that none of us take others as lords beside God. And if they turn away, it says, then say: bear witness that we are Muslims, those who have surrendered. Notice what the verse doesn't do. It doesn't threaten. It invites, names the ground it believes both sides share, and if the answer is no, it simply asks the other side to witness where Muslims stand. Commentators such as Ibn Kathir connect this part of the surah to a delegation of Christians from Najran who came to Medina to talk with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. And a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari reports that when the Prophet wrote to Heraclius, the Byzantine emperor, his letter included this very verse. The 2007 letter took the same phrase and built on two commandments it found in both scriptures: love of God, and love of neighbor. Christian leaders wrote back, and meetings followed. Muslims and Christians still differ on central things, and the verse itself names some of them. But it opens with the word common. It starts the conversation from what is shared.
screen: `KALIMATIN SAWA': A LEVEL WORD` · `AHL AL-KITAB: PEOPLE OF THE SCRIPTURE` · `AN INVITATION, NOT A THREAT` · `FROM HERACLIUS TO 2007` · then, large: `COME TO A COMMON WORD.`

segments.voice: When the bell starts, bring to mind a neighbor, a coworker or a relative whose beliefs aren't yours. Picture a table between the two of you. Instead of setting your differences on it, set down, one at a time, the things you both care about: the people you love, honesty, a good day's work, maybe a God you each pray to in your own way. Look at what's on the table. Find one sentence you could both say and mean. Hold it. The bell holds the time.
A common word. Kalimatin sawa', a word level between us, the invitation of 3:64 to the People of the Scripture. Today's word.
Your line: a common word. Today, in one conversation that could turn into an argument, start by saying out loud the thing you both agree on. Day three hundred sixty-eight.

369.title: The rope of Allah
369.hook: hold fast together to the rope of Allah and don't divide (3:103)
369.howItsDone: Muslims often quote 3:103 in sermons and community gatherings as a call to unity, and many read the 'rope of Allah' as the Qur'an, the shared book that holds the community together.

segments.voice: Yesterday: come to a common word, level between us and you. Your line was a common word. Did you start a hard conversation from shared ground? Day three hundred sixty-nine.

Before the Prophet ﷺ came to Medina, the city had two great Arab tribes, the Aws and the Khazraj. The reports call them kin, and they had a long history of feuds and revenge, ending in a battle called Bu'ath not long before. Then both tribes became Muslim, and they sat in the same rows to pray. That's a huge thing to ask of people with dead relatives between them. The verse for today was spoken into that room.
screen: `TWO TRIBES OF MEDINA.` → `A LONG FEUD.` → `THE SAME ROWS TO PRAY.`

segments.voice: Pickthall translates 3:103: "And hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate." Cable, rope, the Arabic is habl: a rope you hold so you don't fall. And all of you together is part of the command. It isn't a rope for one person to cling to alone. The verse goes on: remember God's favor to you, how you were enemies, and He joined your hearts, and by His grace you became brothers. You were on the edge of a pit of fire, and He saved you from it. Commentators hear the Aws and the Khazraj in it, though the verse names no one. Commentators tell a story, found in the major tafsir works, of a man who tried to reopen the old wound by having someone recite poems from the war days. Tempers flared, hands went to weapons, and the Prophet came out and reminded them who they now were. What is the rope? Commentators give several answers. Some say the Qur'an itself, and a report in Tirmidhi has the Prophet call the Book of God a rope stretched from heaven to earth. Others say the covenant with God, or the community of believers, or sincere faith. These answers don't fight each other: a rope is something many hands can hold at once. And notice the picture. A rope doesn't make everyone stand in the same spot. People hold it at different points, some near, some far. The only thing it asks is that you don't let go, and that you don't cut it.
screen: `HABL: A ROPE YOU HOLD` · `ALL OF YOU, TOGETHER` · `ENEMIES MADE BROTHERS` · `WHAT IS THE ROPE?` · then, large: `HOLD FAST, AND DO NOT SEPARATE.`

segments.voice: When the bell starts, picture your own circle: family, friends, a mosque, a team at work. Somewhere in it there's a split, small or old. Two people who don't talk, or you and someone you've drifted from. Picture a single rope that both of you are holding at different points. You don't have to fix everything today. Just ask yourself what one small pull back toward each other would look like: a message, a greeting, a kind word about them to someone else. The bell holds the time.
The rope of Allah. Habl Allah, held by everyone together, in 3:103, with the command not to divide. Today's word.
Your line: hold the rope together. Today, take one step to mend one split in your circle, even if it's only a hello. Day three hundred sixty-nine.

370.title: Calling to good
370.hook: let there be a people inviting to good and forbidding wrong (3:104)
370.howItsDone: Muslims describe enjoining good and forbidding wrong as a communal duty; in practice it ranges from encouraging prayer and charity to gently advising friends, with scholars stressing knowledge, gentleness and avoiding greater harm.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rope of Allah, held by everyone together. Your line was hold the rope together. Did you take one step to mend a split? Day three hundred seventy.

Every group chat has one. The person who posts the fundraiser link, reminds everyone it's someone's birthday, suggests visiting the friend in the hospital, and, now and then, says gently, maybe let's not share that. Sometimes people roll their eyes. The group would miss them if they left. The very next verse after the rope of Allah describes a whole community of people like that, and gives them a job description.
screen: `THE ONE IN THE GROUP CHAT.` → `THE BIRTHDAY, THE HOSPITAL VISIT.` → `A JOB DESCRIPTION.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's translation, 3:104 says: "And there may spring from you a nation who invite to goodness, and enjoin right conduct and forbid indecency. Such are they who are successful." The famous Arabic phrase inside it is al-amr bil-ma'ruf wan-nahy 'an al-munkar: enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong. Listen to the two key words. Ma'ruf comes from a root meaning to know. The good here is the recognized good, the kind decent people know when they see it. Munkar, the wrong, is what's rejected, what people recognize as not right. And the verse starts with invite. Invitation comes first, the open door, before any correcting. Scholars noticed a small word too: min, from you. Does it mean a group among you should do this, or that all of you should be this kind of people? Some classical scholars read it as some among you, a duty a part of the community fulfills for everyone. Others read it as describing the whole community. A well-known hadith in Sahih Muslim sets out the steps. Whoever sees a wrong, let him change it with his hand; if he can't, then with his tongue; if he can't, then in his heart, and that is the weakest of faith. Scholars such as al-Ghazali attached conditions: know the matter well, act gently, and don't cause a greater harm than the one you're stopping. So the verse isn't a license to police strangers. It begins with the person who invites, and the good it means is the kind everyone recognizes.
screen: `INVITE, ENJOIN, FORBID` · `MA'RUF: THE GOOD EVERYONE KNOWS` · `SOME OF YOU, OR ALL OF YOU?` · `HAND, TONGUE, HEART` · then, large: `A PEOPLE WHO INVITE TO GOODNESS.`

segments.voice: When the bell starts, think of one good thing already happening around you that could use a push. A cousin's small business, a friend's effort to quit something, a neighbor organizing a food drive, a child practicing an instrument. Picture the person. Then picture yourself encouraging them: the exact words, the message, the way you'd say it. Keep it warm and specific. You're not correcting anyone today. You're inviting good to grow. The bell holds the time.
Calling to good. A people who invite to goodness, enjoin the ma'ruf, the good that's known, and forbid the wrong, from 3:104. Today's word.
Your line: invite to good. Today, send that encouragement you just pictured, one real message to one real person doing something good. Day three hundred seventy.

371.title: Don't lose heart
371.hook: after Uhud: don't weaken or grieve, days of fortune rotate among people (3:139–140)
371.howItsDone: Muslims remember Uhud and its martyrs, including Hamzah, the Prophet's uncle, and the verses of Al 'Imran revealed after the battle are often recited for comfort after loss and defeat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a people who invite to good: the ma'ruf, the good everyone knows. Your line was invite to good. Did you send that message of encouragement? Day three hundred seventy-one, the end of a week.

A year after their first victory at Badr, the Muslims of Medina met a much larger army from Mecca at the foot of a mountain called Uhud. The battle started well. Then a group of archers, told by the Prophet ﷺ never to leave their hill, saw the enemy running and came down for the spoils. The cavalry swept around behind them. Many Muslims died, among them the Prophet's uncle Hamzah, and the Prophet himself was wounded. They walked home to a city in mourning.
screen: `THE MOUNTAIN OF UHUD.` → `THE ARCHERS LEAVE THE HILL.` → `A CITY IN MOURNING.`

segments.voice: A large part of Al 'Imran, from around verse 121 on, speaks into the days after that loss. It doesn't pretend the defeat didn't happen, and it doesn't hide the mistake. But in 3:139 it says, in Pickthall's words: "Faint not nor grieve." Then 3:140 gives the reason, and it's surprising. If a wound has touched you, a wound like it touched the other side too, at Badr. And then the line: these are the days, and We make them take turns among people. The verb is nudawiluha, from a root, d-w-l, that means to rotate, to pass from hand to hand. The same root gives the Arabic word dawla, which today means a state, a country, but at heart means a turn: power is something that rotates. So the verse doesn't promise you'll always win. It says the days turn, for everyone. Good days and bad days are passed around, and neither one stays forever. The verse adds that this is how God makes known who truly believes, and takes witnesses, shuhada, from among them: the martyrs of Uhud. There's grief in it, and dignity. Look back at this week and you can see the surah building toward this. A chosen family whose choosing meant a weight to carry. Zakariyya's silence. Maryam, chosen and purified. A common word. The rope held together. A people who call to good. And now a community that got knocked down, and is told: don't lose heart. The days turn.
screen: `NOT HIDING THE LOSS` · `FAINT NOT NOR GRIEVE` · `D-W-L: THE DAYS TAKE TURNS` · `A WEEK BUILDING TO THIS` · then, large: `THESE ARE THE DAYS.`

segments.voice: When the bell starts, bring to mind a recent loss or setback, small or large. A plan that failed, a bad week, a door that closed. Let yourself feel it honestly; the verse doesn't ask anyone to pretend. Then remember one day in your past that felt just as bad and has since turned, a day you got through. Breathe with both of them. If you pray, you can ask God for steadiness. Then choose one small next step, something you can do tomorrow to keep going. The bell holds the time.
Don't lose heart. Spoken to the Muslims after Uhud: faint not nor grieve, the days take turns among people. Today's word.
Your line: days turn. Today, take that one next step after your setback, and tell yourself the line when the day feels stuck. Day three hundred seventy-one.
